title: Is It Wrong to Be Angry at God?
excerpt: The Bible holds more anger at God than most of its readers have noticed, from the psalms to the prophets to Job. Christians differ on what to call that anger, and agree on where to take it.
body:
A mother buried her son in the spring, and she has stopped praying because the only thing she wants to say to God is something she was taught never to say. A man prayed for his marriage every morning for three years, and it ended anyway, and he sits in the back row now with his arms folded. A college student was told by a youth leader that being angry at God is a kind of blasphemy, so she has learned to say she is fine. An old farmer, asked at his wife's funeral how he was holding up, said quietly that he and the Lord were not on speaking terms just now.

Each of them is angry at God, and each believes, more or less, that the anger itself is a sin they will have to answer for.

The skeptic thinks they have been cheated twice. If God is all-powerful and allowed this, he says, then anger is the reasonable response, and a religion that forbids it is a religion that forbids honesty. You may believe in God, it seems, as long as you agree never to say what you think of him.

He is right that a faith which only allows polite feelings would be a dishonest faith. He is wrong about the Bible. The book Christians call Scripture contains more anger at God than most of its readers have noticed, and most of it is spoken by people God called his own.

Some readers are asking this from somewhere very dark, and the argument below can wait. The page for the person asking [why God would let this happen](/help/suffering) begins by saying you don't have to make sense of it tonight, and it says: "If this has left you not wanting to live, call or text one of the lines just below now." The page on [anger](/help/anger) is for anger of every kind, including the kind aimed at heaven, and [Find Help](/help) has the rest.

## The Prayer Book Has Rage in It

Israel's hymnal is the book of Psalms, and a surprising number of its prayers are complaints. "How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me?" (Psalm 13:1). Another asks God to wake up: "Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord? Rouse yourself! Do not reject us forever!" (Psalm 44:23). These were not private outbursts later tolerated by editors. They were sung, in public, by the gathered people of God.

Psalm 13 moves from complaint to trust in six verses. "But I have trusted in your steadfast love; my heart shall rejoice in your salvation" (Psalm 13:5). The Study Bible's note on [Psalm 13](/study/bible/psalms/13) puts the lesson plainly: "the language of complaint and the language of trust can sit in the same prayer." The psalmist did not stop being angry before he trusted. He trusted while he was still asking how long.

Psalm 88 never gets that far. It is a prayer from the edge of death, and it ends without any turn toward hope: "You have caused my beloved and my friend to shun me; my companions have become darkness" (Psalm 88:18). It accuses God directly. "O LORD, why do you cast my soul away? Why do you hide your face from me?" (Psalm 88:14). And yet it begins by calling him "the God of my salvation," and Israel kept it. The note on [Psalm 88](/study/bible/psalms/88) says what its presence means: "there are seasons of faith in which the only thing left is to keep speaking to God."

The Old Testament scholar Walter Brueggemann, in *The Message of the Psalms* (1984), sorted the psalms into three kinds: songs of orientation, sung when life makes sense; songs of disorientation, sung when it falls apart; and songs of new orientation, sung on the far side of the collapse, by people who have been surprised by God. His point was that the middle kind is not a lapse in the life of faith. It is part of the life of faith, and a church that sings only the first and the last has left its people without words for the season most of them will someday be in.

## Prophets Who Argued

The prophets argued with God too, and some of them did it in language a modern congregation would find shocking. Jeremiah, beaten and put in the stocks for preaching what God had told him to preach, prayed this: "O LORD, you have deceived me, and I was deceived; you are stronger than I, and you have prevailed" (Jeremiah 20:7). A few verses later he cursed the day he was born (Jeremiah 20:14). He could not stop preaching either: if he tried to keep silent, he said, "there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I am weary with holding it in, and I cannot" (Jeremiah 20:9). His anger and his obedience lived in the same man on the same day.

Habakkuk opened his book with a complaint. "O LORD, how long shall I cry for help, and you will not hear?" (Habakkuk 1:2). When God answered that he would send Babylon to punish Judah, Habakkuk complained again, more sharply: "You who are of purer eyes than to see evil and cannot look at wrong, why do you idly look at traitors and remain silent when the wicked swallows up the man more righteous than he?" (Habakkuk 1:13). The book ends with one of the great confessions of faith in the Old Testament, a man resolving to rejoice in God though the fig tree does not blossom and the fields yield no food (Habakkuk 3:17-18). He got there by arguing, not by keeping quiet.

Jonah's anger is the hardest case, and the book seems to know it. God spared Nineveh, the capital of an empire that had done terrible things, and Jonah was furious that he had. "But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was angry" (Jonah 4:1). God did not strike him down. He asked him a question: "Do you do well to be angry?" (Jonah 4:4). Jonah answered that he did, "angry enough to die" (Jonah 4:9). The book ends with God's last question about the city's people and its animals, and we never hear Jonah's reply. Jonah's anger was not righteous; he was angry at God's mercy. But even then God's response was a conversation.

## Job and His Friends

The longest argument with God in the Bible is the book of Job. Job lost his children, his wealth and his health, and spent most of the book protesting that he did not deserve it and demanding that God answer him. "Though he slay me, I will hope in him; yet I will argue my ways to his face" (Job 13:15). His three friends spent most of the book defending God. Job must have sinned, they said; God does not afflict the innocent; Job should stop complaining and repent.

When God finally spoke, he did not explain the suffering. He asked Job questions about the creation, and he rebuked him: "Will you even put me in the wrong? Will you condemn me that you may be in the right?" (Job 40:8). Job answered, "therefore I despise myself, and repent in dust and ashes" (Job 42:6).

Then comes the surprise. God turned to the friends. "My anger burns against you and against your two friends, for you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has" (Job 42:7). The friends, who had defended God, were rebuked; Job, who had accused him, was called his servant and asked to pray for them. The note on [Job 42](/study/bible/job/42) calls this surprising: "the friends, who defended God, are rebuked, and Job, who protested, is called God's servant who spoke accurately."

Readers have argued for centuries about exactly what Job got right. He was not right that God had wronged him, and he repented of some of what he said. But he spoke to God, honestly, from inside his suffering, and he refused to tell lies about God in order to make the suffering easier to explain. The friends spoke about God, confidently, at a safe distance from the pain. It was their tidy theology, not Job's raw prayer, that kindled God's anger.

## Two Answers Christians Give

Faithful Christians answer the question in the title in two ways, and both answers guard something true. The site's page on anger states them side by side, and it is worth doing the same here.

Some say anger at God is never right, because anger is a judgment that someone has done wrong, and God does no wrong. Moses sang of him, "all his ways are justice. A God of faithfulness and without iniquity, just and upright is he" (Deuteronomy 32:4). Paul asked the man who would argue with God's choices, "who are you, O man, to answer back to God?" (Romans 9:20). On this view, what the psalmists model is not anger but grief and bewilderment brought to God, and what Job models at the end is repentance for having accused him. The anger itself should be confessed. The comfort in this answer is real: God can be trusted even when he cannot be understood, and you are not left alone with a God who might be guilty.

Others say anger brought to God can itself be a kind of prayer. They point to the psalms that ask God why he is sleeping, to Jeremiah's "you have deceived me," and above all to God's word that Job, not his friends, had spoken rightly. They don't say God has done wrong. They say that a child who shouts at her father is still talking to her father, and that the Bible seems to prefer that to silence or pretense. The comfort in this answer is real too: you don't have to clean yourself up before you pray.

The two answers are closer than they sound. Both say that God has done no wrong. Both say that honest grief and complaint are welcome in prayer. And the page on anger puts their common ground in one sentence: "Both agree on this much: say it to God rather than walk away from him." This essay doesn't need to settle the remaining question, and it won't pretend the question is easier than it is. Whatever name you give what you are feeling, the place to take it is the same.

## Grumbling in the Tents

There is a kind of anger at God that Scripture does condemn, and it helps to see what it is. In the wilderness, Israel complained often, and many of those complaints were judged severely. Moses, looking back, described one of them: "And you murmured in your tents" (Deuteronomy 1:27). Paul, centuries later, warned the church at Corinth not to "grumble, as some of them did and were destroyed by the Destroyer" (1 Corinthians 10:10).

The difference between that grumbling and the psalmist's complaint is not the strength of the feeling. It is where the feeling goes. The psalmist says "How long, O LORD?" to God's face. The grumbling in the tents was said about God, behind his back, among people who had already decided he could not be trusted and were planning to go back to Egypt. One is the anger of someone who still expects an answer. The other is the contempt of someone who has stopped expecting anything.

That is the real danger in anger at God, and those who warn against it are right to warn. Anger that is not brought to God tends to harden. It becomes a settled conclusion about him, repeated to ourselves and to others until it is the most familiar thing we know about God. The cure is not to suppress it. It is to say it to him.

## Where We Have Failed

The church has often taught people the opposite. We have treated the angry mourner as a problem to be corrected rather than a person to sit beside. We have handed grieving people sentences like "everything happens for a reason" and expected them to be grateful. We have built Sunday mornings in which nearly every song is a song of orientation, and then wondered why people in the middle of disorientation stopped coming. In many churches the woman who has buried her son learns quickly that her grief is welcome for a few weeks and her anger not at all, so she takes it home, where it has no one to speak to but herself.

C. S. Lewis kept notebooks after his wife died in 1960, later published as *A Grief Observed* (1961), and the book is so unguarded that it first appeared under a pseudonym. In it he admits that his fear was not that God did not exist but that God might not be good. Many Christians have found it more comforting than his calmer books, precisely because it says out loud what they had been told never to say. The church should not have left them to find permission in a notebook. It was already in the Psalter.

I'm a pastor, and I know how much easier it is to answer a hard question than to sit with someone who is asking it. The friends of Job were most helpful in the first week, when they sat with him on the ground and said nothing (Job 2:13). They did harm only when they started explaining.

## If You Are Angry Now

If you are angry at God, say so to God. Out loud, if you can, or on paper. Use the psalms if you don't have words of your own; Psalm 13 is short enough to pray in a minute, and Psalm 88 is there for the nights when you have nothing hopeful to say. You don't have to resolve the anger before you pray. Prayer may be where it begins to change, or it may not change for a long time, and you can keep praying anyway.

Tell one person who will not try to fix it. If the anger is spilling onto the people around you, the page on [anger](/help/anger) has practical help, and a counselor can help you untangle grief from anger and both from guilt. If any of this has become thoughts of not wanting to live, call or text 988 now, or use the lines on [Find Help](/help).

And be patient with yourself about the doctrine. You may not know yet whether what you feel is anger or grief or both, or whether you should confess it or offer it. God knows. He answered Job, and he answered Jonah, and he did not wait for them to have their theology in order before he spoke.

## The Cry from the Cross

The most important angry question in the Bible was asked by Jesus. On the cross, in the dark, he cried out in the words of a psalm: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Mark 15:34). He was quoting Psalm 22, which begins in abandonment, "O my God, I cry by day, but you do not answer" (Psalm 22:2), and ends in praise, because God "has not despised or abhorred the affliction of the afflicted, and he has not hidden his face from him, but has heard, when he cried to him" (Psalm 22:24).

The letter to the Hebrews says that in the days of his flesh Jesus "offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to him who was able to save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverence" (Hebrews 5:7). Loud cries and tears, and reverence, in the same sentence. Christians believe that the Son of God has prayed the prayer of the forsaken, and that God did not turn away from it. Whatever you are feeling, you are not the first person to say it to God, and you are not saying it to a God who has never felt it.

The mother who stopped praying may find that what she was taught never to say is already written in her Bible, in a psalm God's people have sung for thousands of years. The farmer who is not on speaking terms with the Lord may find that the Lord is still speaking to him. The God of Job did not ask for silence. He asked to be spoken to, and when he answered, the person he praised was the one who had been arguing with him.

*"How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever?"* (Psalm 13:1)

*"He has not hidden his face from him, but has heard, when he cried to him."* (Psalm 22:24)
